To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lesson observations are not a panacea for improving the quality of teaching and learning.

lesson observations are a complex and multifaceted process, which are influenced by a number of factors, both internal and external to schools, and that the way in which teachers and observers approach and carry out lesson observations has a significant impact on the outcomes and effectiveness of the process.
'Lesson observations can be an effective tool for improving teaching and learning, if used appropriately, but they are not without their problems' (Gorrd Taylor 2012a, 1).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which teachers' lesson observation practice is shaped by the policy context in which it is situated, and the ways in which it is shaped by the teachers themselves.

understanding how the practice of classroom observation is carried out by teachers in England, how it is used in schools to improve the quality of teaching and how teachers' views on classroom observation are shaped by the way they are observed.
how teachers and headteachers use the information from lesson observations in their school to inform their professional practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

'the world of educational research is not exclusively quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods, it is a complex, mixed, messy, multi-layered, multi-faceted, multi-dimensional, multi-angled, multi-epistemological, multi-ontological, multi-methodological world' (Gorall Taylor 2004) I have chosen to use the term'mixed world' rather than'mixed method' to emphasise the complexity and multi-dimensionality of the research process.
'mixed methods is the future of educational research' (Tashakkori Teddlie 2010, 2) and it is this approach that I will be drawing upon for this presentation.
I am a mixed methods researcher, but I am not a mixed methodologist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we used a mixed methods approach to explore the use and value of lesson observations in the UK, with a particular focus on their impact on teachers and their professional development.

it is 'a systematic investigation into a social or natural phenomenon using statistical, mathematical, or logical methods' (OED 2015) and that 'it is the search for general truths, which is the opposite of case studies, which are the search for specific facts' (OED, 2015).
we are 'interested in the interplay of quantitative and qualitative research, the combination of the two, and the ways that they can be integrated' (Cohen et al 2011, xvi)
The main takeaway from our work is that

we need to be aware that the way we do research has a significant influence on the findings that we get and that the way we interpret those findings has a major bearing on what we conclude and how we report our findings.
there are a range of different approaches to lesson observation and that there is a need for a more open and inclusive discussion around the topic.

we need a more nuanced understanding of the nature of lesson observation, one that is sensitive to the different ways in which it can be used, and one that takes account of the different perspectives of teachers and observers.
